overview: Buzzers come in two functionally different types that look almost identical, and mixing them up is the most common beginner confusion: an active buzzer has its own internal oscillator, so applying any steady DC voltage makes it beep at one fixed pitch — dead simple, but you can't change the tone. A passive buzzer has no internal oscillator at all; it just vibrates at whatever frequency you feed it, meaning it needs a PWM/tone signal from the microcontroller to make any sound, but in exchange it can play actual musical notes and melodies, not just a single beep.
simpleSummary: A small speaker-like part that beeps — either on its own fixed tone or playing any tone your code sends it.

specifications.activeType: Internal oscillator, fixed pitch, driven by steady DC — just needs HIGH/LOW
specifications.passiveType: No internal oscillator, needs a PWM/tone signal at the desired frequency to produce sound
specifications.soundOutput: ~85-100 dB typical for small piezo/magnetic buzzers

pinMap.name: Positive (+)
pinMap.function: Positive terminal — often marked with a longer lead or a '+' symbol.
pinMap.gotcha: Active and passive buzzers are frequently visually identical — if code that plays a melody produces only a single tone (or vice versa), you likely have the wrong type.

useCases.title: Alarm/alert sound
useCases.scenario: An active buzzer wired to a digital pin for a simple on/off alert tone.

useCases.title: Melody/musical notification
useCases.scenario: A passive buzzer driven with the tone() function to play simple melodies or distinct notification sounds.

useCases.title: Sonar-style distance feedback
useCases.scenario: Vary a passive buzzer's pitch based on a distance sensor reading, like a parking sensor.

oftenConfusedWith: Small speakers (buzzers are single-frequency-capable at best, not full audio)
oftenUpgradedTo: A small speaker + audio amplifier for actual audio playback
